pages.title: What this unit is about
pages.body:
> 📝 **Strand 2 — Productivity Software**
Sub-strand 1: Introduction to Word Processing

Tables organise information neatly, hyperlinks connect documents to the web, and page formatting makes long documents professional. In this unit you will master all three in Microsoft Word.

pages.title: Content standard and lessons
pages.body:
> 🎯 **Content standard**
- **B8.2.1.1** Demonstrate how to use Microsoft Word (tables and hyperlink pages).

> 🧭 **What you will be able to do**
- **B8.2.1.1.1** Demonstrate how to create a table and hyperlinks.
- **B8.2.1.1.2** Demonstrate how to merge, split, add formula, borders and shades.
- **B8.2.1.1.3** Demonstrate how to format a page (page adjustment, header and footer, page numbers, breaks and orientation).

> 🗺️ **Lessons in this unit**
- 4.1 Creating Tables and Hyperlinks
- 4.2 Merging, Splitting, Formulas, Borders and Shading in Tables
- 4.3 Page Formatting

**Core competencies developed:** Creativity and Innovation (CI5.4), Digital Literacy (DL5.1).

lessons.title: Creating Tables and Hyperlinks

pages.title: Creating Tables and Hyperlinks
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B8.2.1.1.1
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- use the Tables group on the Insert tab;
- create, resize and edit tables;
- insert hyperlinks to create non-linear documents.
A **table** is a grid of **rows** and **columns**; each box is a **cell**. Tables are used for timetables, results, price lists and comparisons.
> 🪜 **Step by step — Inserting a table**
1. Click where the table should go.
2. Click **Insert › Tables › Table** and drag across the grid to choose, e.g., 4 columns × 5 rows. Or click **Insert Table…** and type the numbers.
3. Type in the first cell; press **Tab** to move to the next cell (pressing Tab in the last cell adds a new row).
4. To **resize** a column, drag its border; to make columns equal, select the table and click **Layout › Distribute Columns**; use **AutoFit › AutoFit Contents** to fit text.
5. To add rows or columns, click in the table and use **Layout › Insert Above / Below / Left / Right**; to delete, use **Layout › Delete**.
> ✨ **Did you know?** When you click inside a table, two extra tabs appear: **Table Design** (styles, shading, borders) and **Layout** (rows, columns, merge, split, alignment, formula). These are called **contextual tabs**.
## Hyperlinks and non-linear documents
A **hyperlink** is clickable text or a picture that takes the reader to another place: a web page, another file, an email address or another part of the same document. Hyperlinks make documents **non-linear**: readers can jump to what interests them instead of reading from start to end.

pages.title: Creating Tables and Hyperlinks (continued)
pages.body:
> 🪜 **Step by step — Inserting a hyperlink**
1. Select the text or picture to turn into a link, e.g. NaCCA website.
2. Click **Insert › Links › Link** (or press **Ctrl + K**).
3. Choose: **Existing File or Web Page** and type the address, e.g. https://nacca.gov.gh; or **Place in This Document** and pick a heading or bookmark; or **E-mail Address**.
4. Click **OK**. Hold **Ctrl** and click the link to test it. Right-click › **Edit Link** or **Remove Link** to change it.
> 💻 **Practical session — A non-linear school guide**
Create a one-page “Welcome to Our School” document with a table listing four departments. Make each department name a hyperlink to a heading further down the document (use **Insert › Bookmark** or headings), and add a hyperlink to the Ghana Education Service website.

pages.title: Merging, Splitting, Formulas, Borders and Shading in Tables
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B8.2.1.1.2
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- merge and split cells;
- add formulas to tables;
- apply borders and shading; use bullets, indentation and line spacing.
| **Task** | **How to do it** |
|---|---|
| Merge cells | Select adjacent cells › **Layout › Merge Cells** (e.g. one title cell across the top) |
| Split cells | Click a cell › **Layout › Split Cells**, enter the number of columns and rows |
| Split a table | Click in the row that should begin the new table › **Layout › Split Table** |
| Add a formula | Click the cell for the answer › **Layout › Data › Formula**. Word suggests =SUM(ABOVE) or =SUM(LEFT); other functions include AVERAGE, MAX, MIN. Choose a number format and click **OK** |
| Borders | **Table Design › Borders**: choose line style, weight and colour, then All Borders, Outside Borders, etc.; or use **Border Painter** |
| Shading | **Table Design › Shading**: choose a fill colour for selected cells |
| Table styles | **Table Design › Table Styles**: one-click professional designs |
> 🛡️ **Safety first — Word formulas do not update automatically** Unlike Excel, a formula in a Word table does **not** recalculate when numbers change. Right-click the result and choose **Update Field** (or press **F9**). For heavy calculations, use Excel.

pages.title: Merging, Splitting, Formulas, Borders and Shading in Tables (continued)
pages.body:
Bullets, increase/decrease indent, borders and line spacing (Home › Paragraph and its dialog box launcher) work inside table cells just as in normal paragraphs (see Basic 7, Unit 4).
> 💻 **Practical session — Results table**
Create a table of five learners with columns **Name, Maths, Science, English, Total**. Merge the top row for the title **B8 MID-TERM RESULTS**, use =SUM(LEFT) to total each row, and =AVERAGE(ABOVE) for a class average row. Apply a table style, shade the heading row and centre the numbers.

pages.title: Page Formatting
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B8.2.1.1.3
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- adjust margins, orientation and size;
- insert headers, footers and page numbers;
- insert page and section breaks.
| **Command** | **Where** | **Purpose** |
|---|---|---|
| Margins | Layout › Page Setup › Margins | Normal (2.54 cm), Narrow, Wide, Custom |
| Orientation | Layout › Orientation | Portrait or Landscape |
| Size | Layout › Size | A4 (21 × 29.7 cm), Letter, A3, A5 |
| Columns | Layout › Columns | Newspaper-style columns |
| Header / Footer | Insert › Header & Footer | Text at the top/bottom of every page; double-click the area to edit; **Different First Page** option |
| Page Number | Insert › Page Number | Top or bottom of page; **Format Page Numbers** to start at a given number or use i, ii, iii |
| Page break | Insert › Page Break or **Ctrl + Enter** | Starts a new page |
| Section break | Layout › Breaks › Next Page / Continuous | Allows different orientation, headers or columns in different parts of one document |
> 🪜 **Step by step — Making one landscape page in a portrait document**
1. Place the cursor at the start of the page that should be landscape and insert **Layout › Breaks › Next Page**.
2. Place the cursor at the end of that page and insert another **Next Page** section break.
3. Click inside the middle section and choose **Layout › Orientation › Landscape**. Only that section changes.

pages.title: Page Formatting (continued)
pages.body:
> 💻 **Practical session — Format a project report**
Format a three-page report: Narrow margins on A4; a header with the project title; a footer with “Page X of Y” (Insert › Page Number › Bottom of Page › Page X of Y); a page break before each main section; and the second page in landscape to hold a wide table.

1. Describe how to insert a 3 × 6 table and resize its columns.
2. What is a non-linear document? How do hyperlinks create one?
3. Explain how to merge and split cells.
4. Distinguish between a page break and a section break.
